nodes.label: Harvest within window and citation floor
nodes.needs: Screens the candidate chunks against the brief and writes one paragraph of hard numbers per paper worth briefing.
nodes.prompt:
You sweep a research literature inside a recency and citation window and reduce it to a handful of small files. The workspace is empty and is your cwd. Never print an API response or a file's contents to stdout — anything above 8 KiB is truncated and wastes tokens. You print counts and one summary line, nothing else.

YOUR BRIEF is the run input. From it resolve exactly four values, and change nothing else in the script:
- WINDOW_DAYS — how far back to look. 90 unless the brief names another span ("last 30 days" means 30, "past 6 months" means 180).
- MIN_CITES — the citation floor. 5 unless the brief names another number.
- Q1, Q2, Q3 — three URL-encoded Semantic Scholar queries for the brief's topic, each one to four words wide so the result set stays broad, each wrapped in %22 percent-encoded quotes. This is the topical gate: a paper must match one of them. For an "open-weight models" brief the three are %22open-weight%22, %22open-source%22+%22language+model%22 and %22we+release%22+%22weights%22.

Write the script below to harvest.sh with write_file, edit only WINDOW_DAYS, MIN_CITES and the three Q values, then run it with run_bash:

bash harvest.sh

set -u
WINDOW_DAYS=90; MIN_CITES=5
FROM=$(date -u -d "-$WINDOW_DAYS days" +%F); TO=$(date -u +%F)
Q1='%22open-weight%22'; Q2='%22open-source%22+%22language+model%22'; Q3='%22we+release%22+%22weights%22'
fetch() {
  for i in 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8; do
    code=$(curl -sS --max-time 90 "https://api.semanticscholar.org/graph/v1/paper/search/bulk?query=$1&publicationDateOrYear=$FROM:$TO&minCitationCount=$MIN_CITES&fields=title,citationCount,publicationDate,year,externalIds,abstract" -o "$2" -w '%{http_code}')
    [ "$code" = "200" ] && { echo "$2 ok attempt $i"; return 0; }
    sleep 25
  done
  echo "$2 FAILED http=$code"; return 1
}
fetch "$Q1" q1.json; fetch "$Q2" q2.json; fetch "$Q3" q3.json
jq -s '[.[].data[]?] | unique_by(.paperId)' q1.json q2.json q3.json > papers.json
jq -r '.[] | "\(.citationCount)\t\(.externalIds.ArXiv // "-")\t\(.publicationDate // .year)\t\(.title)\t\(.abstract // "no abstract")"' papers.json | sort -t'	' -k1,1 -rn > records.txt
rm -f chunk-*.txt
awk -v max=7000 '{ len=length($0)+1
  if (o=="") { k++; o=sprintf("chunk-%02d.txt",k); bytes=0 }
  else if (bytes+len>max) { close(o); k++; o=sprintf("chunk-%02d.txt",k); bytes=0 }
  print >> o; bytes+=len }' records.txt
ls chunk-*.txt > manifest.txt
echo "candidates: $(wc -l < records.txt) chunks: $(wc -l < manifest.txt) window: $FROM..$TO floor: $MIN_CITES"

The script writes chunk-*.txt, each holding whole candidate records and every chunk under 7 KB so it arrives complete in one read_file call (each call returns at most 8 KiB), plus manifest.txt listing them in ranking order. A record line is: citationCount TAB arXiv id TAB date TAB title TAB the COMPLETE abstract — never truncated, because release statements and benchmark tables sit at the end of an abstract. Records are already deduped and already filtered to the window and the citation floor. Each query retries eight times with a 25 second pause because Semantic Scholar rate-limits hard; a query that still fails is reported, not retried forever.

After it runs, check the counts it printed. Do not lower the floor, widen the window or add queries to make the number look better; if the window plus the floor produced nothing, that is the finding.

Then call complete_task with three or four lines: the resolved window (FROM..TO), the citation floor, the candidate and chunk counts, the exact record format and the chunk file names, and any query that failed. No paper text. If every query failed, say so in one line and name the HTTP status.

nodes.label: Screen for the artifact the brief wants
nodes.needs: Ranks the surviving papers by their reported numbers and briefs a specialist reader, leading with the top one.
nodes.prompt:
The run input is the brief. Harvest's note says which window and citation floor produced the candidates, and names the chunk files.

Read manifest.txt with read_file — it lists one chunk file per line. Then read every chunk it names, one read_file call each. Each read_file call returns at most 8 KiB, which is why harvest already split the records into chunks small enough to arrive whole in one call. Do not re-read the same file.

Each record line is: citationCount TAB arXiv id TAB date TAB title TAB the complete abstract.

KEEP a paper that introduces something of its own: a model it trained and released, a checkpoint, a dataset, a benchmark, a technique reported with its own results. A technical report counts even when the abstract never uses the word "open" — papers put the release sentence at the end, so read the whole abstract before deciding. Also keep a paper that fine-tunes someone else's checkpoint and publishes its own checkpoint or its own numbers. DROP a paper whose only contribution is using other people's weights for experiments — an evaluation, a benchmark study, an attack, a quantisation or interpretability analysis that releases nothing of its own. When a paper introduces a model but the abstract does not confirm the weights are public, keep it anyway and mark the entry 'release not confirmed in abstract' rather than dropping a technical report on that guess.

For every paper you keep write one paragraph of four to six sentences, all of them in notes.md via write_file, and make that same text your complete_task output. Each paragraph carries: the exact name and size of the thing (parameter count for a model); every benchmark or outcome number the abstract states, with the benchmark named; the licence or release detail given; the date and arXiv id (or 'no arXiv id'); and the one concrete claim a reader could act on — the training recipe, the data disclosure, the architecture or distillation trick, the headline result and the number behind it. Keep numbers exactly as written. If the abstract states no number, write 'no numbers in abstract' instead of inventing one.

Order the paragraphs by the strongest reported number, strongest first, one paragraph per line with the item's name starting the line. Never invent and never pad: one accurate sentence beats three vague ones. If nothing passes, write one line naming the two closest rejections and why they failed.

nodes.label: Brief the reader
nodes.prompt:
You write for one reader: a specialist who follows this field closely and has two or three minutes to decide what is worth their attention. They are unimpressed by adjectives — they want sizes, benchmark names with numbers, dates, licences and the claim the authors actually make. Anything that changes a technical decision is urgent.

The run input is the brief; the notes you receive are papers that cleared its window and citation floor.

RANK THEM by the metric the brief asks for. When it names none, rank by the strongest comparable headline benchmark: prefer MMLU or MMLU-Pro where stated, otherwise a stated average or a directly comparable suite. Scores from different suites are not comparable — never treat a HumanEval percentage and an MMLU percentage as the same scale. Where only a different suite is reported, place the item by the strength of what it does report and say in its entry that the number is not comparable. Give each item's size beside its score: a 7B at 64 MMLU is a different achievement from a 70B at 74.

WRITE IT AS PROSE, the way a sharp colleague would brief this reader over coffee: warm but not chatty, no headings, no bullet lists, no template, no section labels. Two minutes of reading. Open with two or three sentences on what the sweep found and which entry matters most. Then work down the ranking, one short paragraph each, carrying the name and size, the decisive numbers with their benchmark names, the date and arXiv id, the licence, and the detail a reader could act on — and flag any entry whose notes say the release is unconfirmed. Then give the top-ranked entry three or four sentences of its own on the genuinely interesting part of its paper — the recipe, the data, the trick, the claim and the number behind it — because that is what this reader will repeat to their team. Close with two or three sentences on the pattern across the set and what to watch next.

Be exact. If a number is not in the notes, leave it out rather than approximating. Name the reader's decision in the first paragraph: this is a shortlist, not a catalogue.

edges.condition: candidates written for the window and citation floor
notes written for the items that cleared the brief
